patients.summary: Administrative assistant on Medicaid with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and severe obesity who joins in 2021, has a Roux-en-Y bypass in 2022 complicated by an anastomotic leak, then in 2025-2026 is found to have Cushing syndrome with an L1 fracture, a gastrojejunal stricture, B12 deficiency anemia, erysipelas and septic cavernous sinus thrombosis. Endocrinology localization of the Cushing syndrome is the open thread at today.

- Type 2 diabetes, on metformin 1000 mg BID. Last A1c in their records 8.9 (spring 2021).

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

45F transferring care from another primary care office (records reviewed, in chart). Wants a doctor she can actually reach; her last office kept changing providers on her.

HPI: Type 2 DM dx about 8 years ago, on metformin 1000 BID, never on anything else. Says she takes it most days, GI upset when she started but settled. Doesn't check sugars, no meter at home. Last A1c in outside records 8.9. HTN on lisinopril 20, no side effects. Weight has been 115-120 kg for years. Has tried calorie counting, a commercial program twice, walking at lunch. Loses 5-8 kg then it comes back. Asking about weight loss surgery, her insurance covers it now and a coworker had it done.
Also gets sinus infections a couple of times a year, usually treated with antibiotics at urgent care. None now.

PMH: T2DM, HTN, obesity, recurrent sinusitis
PSH: none
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily
Allergies: NKDA
FHx: mother T2DM. Father HTN. Maternal aunt with severe obesity.
SHx: Administrative assistant at a property management office. Lives alone in an apartment in town. Never smoker, no alcohol, no drugs.

ROS: no chest pain, dyspnea, polyuria, vision change, numbness of the feet. Snoring per a past partner, no witnessed apneas known.

Exam: vitals in flowsheet. Ht 163 cm, wt 118 kg, BMI 44.4.
Well appearing, pleasant. HEENT normal, no sinus tenderness. Neck supple, no thyromegaly. Heart RRR no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen obese, soft, nontender. Ext no edema. Feet: skin intact, monofilament intact bilaterally, DP pulses 2+.

A/P:
1. Type 2 diabetes, not at goal. A1c today. Discussed options including adding a second agent; she would rather pursue bariatric surgery first, which is reasonable given BMI over 40 with comorbidities. Continue metformin.
2. Hypertension, controlled on lisinopril 20. CMP, UACR.
3. Severe obesity, BMI 44. Referral to bariatric surgery program placed.
4. Recurrent sinusitis by history, quiet now.
5. HM: Tdap and PCV20 today. HCV and HIV screening once, ordered. Screening mammogram ordered. Pap up to date (2019 co-test negative). Colon screening at 45, will start FIT next year after we see where surgery lands. Flu and COVID booster at a nurse visit in October.

RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Michelle, your labs are back. A1c 8.8, which is about what your old office had, so diabetes is not well controlled yet. Kidney function, potassium, thyroid and blood count all normal. No protein in the urine. LDL cholesterol is a bit high. Hepatitis C and HIV screens negative. The bariatric program should call you in the next couple of weeks; let me know if you don't hear from them.

reports.text: Bilateral digital screening mammogram with tomosynthesis. Comparison: prior outside study 2020. Breast composition: scattered areas of fibroglandular density. No suspicious mass, architectural distortion or suspicious calcifications. Skin and nipples normal. Axillae unremarkable.

documents.title: Bariatric Surgery Consultation
documents.author: bariatric surgery
documents.body:
Regional Bariatric Surgery Program
Date of consultation: 10/19/2021

Thank you for referring Ms. Tremblay, 45, for surgical weight loss evaluation.

She has had obesity since her twenties, with multiple supervised diet attempts. Comorbidities: type 2 diabetes (most recent A1c 8.8), hypertension. No GERD symptoms. Never smoker, no alcohol. Medications metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily. NKDA.

Exam: Ht 163 cm, Wt 117.6 kg, BMI 44.3. BP 132/84. Abdomen obese, soft, no hernias, no prior incisions.

Assessment: Class III obesity with diabetes. Good candidate for laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, which offers the best metabolic benefit for her diabetes. Risks reviewed at length, including leak, stricture, marginal ulcer, internal hernia, dumping and lifelong vitamin and mineral deficiencies requiring supplements and monitoring.

Plan: 6-month program: dietitian visits, psychology evaluation, support group, preoperative clearance from PCP closer to the date. We will send the clearance request.

Bariatric Surgery

documents.title: Discharge Summary - Laparoscopic Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass
documents.author: bariatric surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, bariatric surgery service
Admitted 04/21/2022, discharged 04/23/2022

Procedure 04/21/2022: Laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (antecolic, 150 cm Roux limb, small gastric pouch, stapled gastrojejunostomy). Estimated blood loss minimal. No intraoperative complications. Leak test negative at the end of the case.

Hospital course: Uneventful. Advanced to bariatric clear liquids POD 1, tolerated. Ambulating, pain controlled with oral medication by POD 2. Afebrile, heart rate 70s-80s at discharge. Glucose 120s-150s.

Discharge medications:
- Metformin 1000 mg twice daily (resume)
- Lisinopril 20 mg daily
- Cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily (new, lifelong)
- Calcium carbonate with vitamin D 600 mg/400 units twice daily (new, separate from multivitamin)
- Multivitamin 1 tablet daily, chewable for the first month (new)
Allergies: NKDA

Diet: bariatric full liquid stage for 2 weeks per handout.
Return precautions: fever, increasing abdominal pain, fast heart rate, shortness of breath, vomiting.
Follow-up in bariatric clinic in 2 weeks; PCP in 2-4 weeks.

reports.text: Single upright portable AP view. Lungs are clear without focal consolidation, effusion or pneumothorax. Heart size normal. No free intraperitoneal air beneath the hemidiaphragms. Postsurgical staple lines in the left upper quadrant.
reports.conclusion: No free air under the diaphragm. No acute cardiopulmonary process.

documents.title: Discharge Summary - Anastomotic Leak
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Regional hospital, general surgery
Admitted 04/26/2022 via the emergency department. Discharged 05/06/2022.

Reason for admission: Five days after laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (04/21), two days of worsening abdominal pain, fever and shortness of breath.

Presentation: T 38.7 C, HR 110, RR 22, BP 135/85. Abdomen distended and diffusely tender to palpation; no rebound, no guarding. WBC 14.0, Hgb 12.5, platelets 250, creatinine 1.0, BUN 18, glucose 180. Upright chest film without free air.

Given tachycardia, fever and pain early after bypass, she was taken emergently to the OR the same night.

Procedure 04/26/2022: Diagnostic laparoscopy converted to exploratory laparotomy. Leak identified at the gastrojejunal anastomosis with localized contamination in the left upper quadrant. Primary repair with omental buttress, washout, two closed suction drains placed.

Hospital course: Broad-spectrum IV piperacillin-tazobactam. NPO with IV fluids, then clear liquids from POD 5 and advanced to bariatric full liquids. Metformin held while NPO and resumed on diet. Drains removed POD 8 and 9. Fevers resolved by day 3, white count normalized. Midline incision clean, staples out at bariatric clinic follow-up.

Diagnosis: Anastomotic leak (gastrojejunostomy) after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, repaired.

Discharge medications: unchanged from 04/23 (metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily, calcium carbonate/vitamin D 600 mg/400 units BID, multivitamin daily). Antibiotics completed in hospital.
Allergies: NKDA.
Follow-up: bariatric surgery clinic 1 week; PCP 1 week.

events.reason: Hospital follow-up after gastric bypass and leak repair

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Post-discharge visit. Bypass 4/21, back 4/26 with a leak at the GJ anastomosis, ex-lap and repair, home 5/6. Discharge summary reviewed.

Feels weak and tired but much better. Pain mostly at the midline incision, using less of the pain medicine each day. Tolerating full liquids, protein shakes 3/day, sipping water all day. No fever, no vomiting. BMs every 2 days.

Taking metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 20, B12 1000 mcg, calcium/D BID, multivitamin. Sugars in the hospital 120s-150s.

Exam: afebrile, HR 84, BP ok. Looks tired. Midline incision healing, no erythema or drainage, drain sites dry and closed. Abdomen soft, appropriately tender near incision. Lungs clear.

A/P
1. S/p RYGB complicated by anastomotic leak, repaired. Recovering. Leak resolved per surgery. CBC/BMP today. Bariatric clinic Friday.
2. T2DM: continue metformin for now. If intake stays low and sugars drop, may need to lower; she'll call with any shakiness or sweats.
3. HTN: BP fine, continue lisinopril; may need less as weight falls.
4. Supplements as above, lifelong.
RTC 2-3 months.

documents.title: Bariatric Surgery Follow-up
documents.author: bariatric surgery
documents.body:
Bariatric surgery clinic, 3-month postoperative visit 07/21/2022.

Doing well after a difficult start (leak, repaired). Eating soft solids, small portions, protein goal met most days. No vomiting, no dysphagia, no dumping. Weight 98.6 kg, down from 114 kg preoperatively.

Incision healed. Taking cyanocobalamin, calcium with vitamin D and multivitamin as prescribed.

Plan: continue supplements lifelong. Labs at 6 and 12 months. Annual visits thereafter. Reminder to avoid NSAIDs.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ANNUAL PHYSICAL

46F, 6 months out from RYGB (leak, repaired). Feels like a different person. Down about 25 kg from pre-op, 93 kg today. Eating 3 small meals + protein snacks. Walking 40 min at lunch. No vomiting, no dysphagia, occasional loose stool after sweets which she now avoids. Taking all supplements.
No sinus infections this year.

Meds: metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 20, cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg, calcium/D 600/400 BID, MVI.
Allergies: NKDA

ROS otherwise negative. Periods regular.

Exam: BMI 35.2. Well appearing. HEENT nl. Thyroid nl. Heart RRR, lungs clear. Breasts deferred to mammogram. Abd: healed midline and port scars, soft, NT. Skin: no lesions of concern. Ext no edema. Feet: monofilament intact, pulses 2+.

A/P
- T2DM: A1c today; expect a big improvement. Continue metformin for now.
- HTN: 126/80 on lisinopril 20. Continue.
- S/p RYGB: supplements lifelong, bariatric clinic is checking micronutrients.
- HM: flu + bivalent COVID today. FIT kit given (age 46, average risk). Mammogram due next fall. Pap due 2024. PHQ-2 0.
RTC 6 months.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Michelle, great news: A1c is down to 6.9 from 8.8 last year. Kidney and liver tests normal, blood count normal, urine protein normal. LDL still in the high 120s. Keep up the walking. Remember to send back the FIT kit.

documents.title: Video Visit - Sinusitis
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video visit from her car at work, identity verified, consents to telehealth.

Cold started about 12 days ago, got a little better, now worse for 3 days: R cheek and upper teeth pressure, thick yellow-green drainage, stuffy, low-grade temp to 100.2 last night. No vision change, no eye swelling, no severe headache, no stiff neck. This is her pattern, 1-2 sinus infections a year.
No antibiotics in the past 6 months. NKDA.

Exam over video: speaking full sentences, nasal voice, mild tenderness when she presses on R maxilla, no periorbital swelling or redness.

A/P: Acute bacterial sinusitis (double worsening after initial improvement), in a patient with recurrent sinusitis and diabetes. Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 BID x10 days. Saline rinses. Take with food, separate from calcium by 2 hours if she can. Return precautions: eye swelling, vision change, severe headache, high fever -> call same day or ED.
If more than 3-4 a year, would consider ENT.

documents.title: Weight and Diabetes Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Returns for weight follow-up, 6 months after we made a plan at her physical. Bypass 2022, course complicated by a leak that year.

She has done everything we discussed: low-calorie plan with a food log app, gym 3-4x/week after work since November. Down only 2 kg in 6 months. Clearly frustrated, a little tearful. Feels her belly is bigger even though the scale barely moved; pants tight at the waist, other clothes fit the same. Taking metformin and lisinopril, plus her bariatric supplements.

No polyuria. Sleeping ok. No new meds or OTCs.

Exam: BP 132/86. Wt 90.3 kg, BMI 34. Waist circumference 102 cm. Abdomen protuberant, soft, nontender, scars healed. No edema. Heart/lungs nl.

Labs 4/14 (fasting): glucose 146, A1c 7.2, TC 210, HDL 38, LDL 130, TG 220. Reviewed with her.

A/P
1. Obesity, BMI 34, with weight regain and now a plateau despite a real effort, and weight redistributing to the middle. Adding obesity to the problem list. Given the plateau and central pattern in a woman with diabetes and hypertension, would like endocrinology to evaluate before anything else. Referral placed.
2. T2DM: A1c 7.2, drifting up. Continue metformin 1000 BID for now; revisit after endo.
3. HTN: 132/86, ok on lisinopril 20.
4. Lipids reviewed.
RTC after endo visit.

reports.text: AP and lateral views of the thoracolumbar junction and lumbar spine. Anterior wedge compression deformity of the L1 vertebral body. Posterior vertebral body line intact. No lytic or blastic lesion, no endplate erosion, no paraspinal soft tissue mass. Remaining vertebral heights preserved. Disc spaces maintained. Alignment normal.
reports.conclusion: Anterior wedge compression fracture of L1. No radiographic evidence of malignancy or infection.

documents.title: Endocrinology Consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology consultation. Date of visit 05/19/2025.
Referred by her primary care physician for central weight gain and a weight-loss plateau after gastric bypass.

History: 48-year-old woman (49 next month) with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in 2022 complicated by an anastomotic leak. About two weeks ago she reached up to a high shelf for a heavy box, twisted, felt something give way in her mid-back with a pop, and has had severe pain there since. No fall, no major trauma. Separately, for several months she has noticed her middle getting bigger, which she connects to a stressful stretch in her life. Energy is low and she tires easily.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily, calcium carbonate/vitamin D twice daily, multivitamin. No glucocorticoids of any kind, by mouth, inhaled, injected or topical.
Allergies: NKDA. Never smoker, no alcohol or drugs.

Exam: Purplish striae across the lower abdomen and upper thighs. Tender to palpation over the thoracolumbar spine; range of motion limited by pain. Neurologically intact in the legs.

Results:
8 AM cortisol 29 ug/dL
24-hour urine free cortisol 388 ug/day
Fasting glucose 132 mg/dL
Calcium 9.2 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase 138 U/L
Thoracolumbar films: anterior wedge compression fracture at L1, no features of malignancy or infection.
DXA: decreased bone mineral density.

Assessment:
1. Cushing syndrome. Clinical features (central weight gain, violaceous striae, low-trauma vertebral fracture with low bone density, worsening glucose) with a markedly elevated urine free cortisol and high morning cortisol, no exogenous steroid exposure.
2. L1 compression fracture with decreased bone density, consistent with cortisol excess.

Plan: Diagnosis discussed with her. Continue calcium and vitamin D. Activity as tolerated for the back. Will see her back in clinic.

Endocrinology

documents.title: Endocrinology appointment
documents.author: patient
documents.body: The endocrinologist said I have Cushing's. I looked it up and I'm kind of freaked out. Can I come in to talk about it? My back is still killing me too.

documents.title: Follow-up - Endocrinology Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here to talk through the endocrinology consult. Endo letter of 5/19 reviewed: high 8 AM cortisol and 24-h urine free cortisol, striae, L1 wedge compression fracture on films, low bone density on DXA. Diagnosis Cushing syndrome.

She was scared after reading online. We went over what it means: her body is making too much cortisol, which explains the belly weight, the stretch marks, the fracture and some of the sugar drift. The endocrinologist will be the one to sort out where it's coming from and how to treat it.

Back: pain 4/10, better than 3 weeks ago. Working, sitting with a lumbar pillow. No leg numbness or weakness, no bladder or bowel change.

Exam: BP and weight in flowsheet. Mild tenderness at thoracolumbar junction. Strength 5/5 legs, reflexes symmetric, gait normal.

1. Cushing syndrome, new per endocrinology. Endo follow-up pending on their end.
2. L1 compression fracture with low bone density. Improving. Continue calcium/vitamin D. Heat, walking, avoid heavy lifting.
3. T2DM, HTN: unchanged plan.
RTC at physical in the fall.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Gastroenterology consultation, visit date 10/21/2025.
Reason for referral: bloating, diarrhea and weight loss after gastric bypass.

HPI: 49-year-old woman, about three and a half years out from Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (anastomotic leak, repaired) and recently diagnosed with Cushing syndrome by endocrinology. Six months of bloating, flatulence and watery diarrhea. She has lost 10 pounds over that time without changing what she eats or how much she exercises. Denies fever, vomiting, hematochezia or melena.
PMH also: type 2 diabetes, well controlled on metformin; hypertension.
Meds: metformin, lisinopril, cyanocobalamin, calcium/vitamin D, multivitamin. NKDA. Never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: Abdomen mildly distended, diffusely tender on palpation without rebound or guarding. Hyperactive bowel sounds. Well-healed laparotomy and port scars.

Data: Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 101 fL, serum B12 150 pg/mL (low despite daily oral supplement), fasting glucose 98 mg/dL. Stool for ova and parasites negative; C. difficile toxin negative.

Assessment: Post-bypass bloating and diarrhea with weight loss; anemia with low B12.
Plan:
1. Upper endoscopy to evaluate the gastric pouch, anastomosis and Roux limb. Scheduled 11/04.
2. Low B12 and anemia: recommend hematology evaluation; we will let the PCP place the referral.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Upper Endoscopy with Balloon Dilation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Procedure: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with through-the-scope balloon dilation. Date 11/04/2025.
Indication: bloating, diarrhea, weight loss after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care. ASA II.

Findings:
- Esophagus: normal mucosa, normal Z-line.
- Gastric pouch: small, normal mucosa.
- Gastrojejunal anastomosis: stricture, estimated 9 mm diameter; the standard endoscope passed with resistance. No marginal ulcer, no staples or sutures exposed.
- Roux limb: normal as far as examined.
Intervention: CRE balloon dilation of the anastomosis to 15 mm, held 60 seconds. Minimal expected oozing. Scope then passed easily.
Complications: none.

Impression: Anastomotic stricture at the gastrojejunostomy, dilated to 15 mm.
Recommendations: liquids today, advance to usual diet tomorrow. Call for chest pain, fever or vomiting.

orders.reason: Anemia with low vitamin B12 after gastric bypass

documents.title: GI results and next step
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Michelle, I have the GI letter and the endoscopy report. They found a narrowing where the stomach pouch joins the intestine and stretched it open. Your blood count is a little low and your B12 level is low even though you take it every day, so GI suggested you see hematology. I've placed that referral; their office will call. Keep taking your B12 until they see you.

documents.title: RE: GI results and next step
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Ok thanks. Eating feels a bit easier since the scope. Still running to the bathroom though. Hematology's first opening is end of December.

documents.title: Hematology Consultation
documents.author: hematology
documents.body:
Hematology consultation. Seen 12/29/2025 at the request of her primary care physician.

HPI: 49-year-old woman after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (2022; leak, repaired) with a recently dilated gastrojejunal anastomotic stricture. Three months of steadily worsening tiredness, generalized weakness and a sore tongue. Takes cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg by mouth daily.
PMH: type 2 diabetes on metformin, hypertension on lisinopril, Cushing syndrome.
Social: no alcohol. Eats little meat, eggs or dairy.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: Pale. Tongue smooth and beefy red. Vibration sense reduced in both feet and ankles. Romberg positive.

Labs: Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 115 fL. Serum B12 150 pg/mL. Folate 4 ng/mL (low). Homocysteine elevated. Methylmalonic acid elevated.

Assessment: Macrocytic anemia from vitamin B12 deficiency (confirmed by raised MMA and homocysteine) with low folate, in the setting of gastric bypass and a diet low in animal products. Posterior column signs.

Plan:
1. Folic acid 1 mg daily.
2. Continue oral cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily.
3. Recheck in 3 weeks with CBC, reticulocytes, B12 and folate.

Hematology

medications.sig: Inject 1 mL (1000 mcg) into the muscle once weekly for 4 doses, then once monthly

documents.title: Hematology Follow-up
documents.author: hematology
documents.body:
Hematology follow-up, seen 01/19/2026.

Still tired and weak, tongue still sore, despite taking oral B12 and the folic acid daily. Weight down 5 kg over the past 3 months.

Exam: Pale. Tongue smooth and beefy red. Neurologic exam normal today.

Labs: Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 115 fL, reticulocytes 1.5%, B12 180 pg/mL, folate 12 ng/mL.

Assessment: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia not responding to oral replacement after gastric bypass; folate now replete.

Plan:
1. Stop oral cyanocobalamin. Cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg IM given in clinic today; then weekly x3 more and monthly thereafter, lifelong. Primary care office has agreed to give the injections.
2. Continue folic acid 1 mg daily.
3. CBC and B12 in about 3 months; can be drawn at her PCP.

Hematology

documents.title: Emergency Department Visit
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Emergency Department record. Date of service 02/27/2026, arrival 18:50.

CC: fever and red, painful right leg.

HPI: 49-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, Cushing syndrome, prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, now on B12 injections for B12 deficiency. Two days of high fevers with shaking chills and a painful red rash on the right lower leg that began as a small red patch and has spread quickly. No injury she recalls. No prior episodes.
Meds (per patient and pharmacy list): metformin, lisinopril, cyanocobalamin, folic acid, calcium/vitamin D, multivitamin.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: T 38.7 C, HR 102, BP 135/85. Right lower leg: bright red, warm, tender, raised plaque with sharply demarcated edges over the anterior and lateral shin. No purulence, no fluctuance, no crepitus, no bullae. Rest of the exam unremarkable.

Labs: WBC 14,000, CRP 25 mg/L. Blood cultures x2 drawn: no growth to date at time of discharge.

MDM: Erysipelas of the right lower leg, presumed streptococcal. No abscess to drain. Febrile but hemodynamically stable, tolerating oral intake, reliable follow-up. Cefazolin 2 g IV given. Fever and heart rate improved on recheck.

Disposition: Discharged 23:15. Penicillin V potassium 500 mg four times daily x10 days. Outline of redness marked with pen. Elevate the leg. Return for spreading beyond the line, worsening fever, confusion or vomiting. PCP follow-up in 2-3 days.

Addendum 03/04: Blood cultures final, no growth at 5 days.

Emergency Medicine

2. B12 deficiency on injections; monthly dose due 3/10, will do here.
3. Cushing syndrome: reminded her to call endocrinology, she has not been back since May.
Call if worse.

reports.text: MRI of the brain and orbits before and after gadolinium, with contrast-enhanced MR venography. Both cavernous sinuses are expanded with filling defects and absent normal enhancement, consistent with thrombosis. Bilateral proptosis with preseptal and periorbital soft tissue swelling. No orbital or intracranial abscess. No subdural or epidural collection. Brain parenchyma normal in signal without infarct or hemorrhage. Ventricles normal in size. Dural venous sinuses otherwise patent.
reports.conclusion: Bilateral cavernous sinus thrombosis. No abscess.

documents.title: Discharge Summary - Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Regional hospital, neurology service (neuro ICU 3/30 to 4/3)
Admitted 03/30/2026. Discharged 04/13/2026.

Presenting history: Three days of severe, constant, worsening headache that hurts more with eye movement, with fever, swelling around both eyes, blurred vision and double vision. Several days before, she squeezed a pimple on her upper lip. ED visit for right leg erysipelas a month ago, treated. PMH: poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, Cushing syndrome, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, B12 deficiency on injections, hypertension, recurrent sinusitis.
Allergies: NKDA.

Admission exam: T 38.7 C, BP 130/85, HR 102, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air. Both eyelids swollen and red, chemosis, proptosis. Visual acuity reduced in both eyes. Eye movements painful and limited in every direction. Pupils react sluggishly. Reduced sensation over forehead and nose. Papilledema both eyes on fundoscopy. Neck supple, no photophobia.

Admission labs: WBC 15,000, hemoglobin 13.2, platelets 250,000, glucose 280, CRP 24 mg/L, ESR 55 mm/hr.

Imaging: Contrast MRI of the brain and orbits with MR venography (3/30): bilateral cavernous sinus thrombosis, no abscess.

Hospital course:
- Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis from a facial source. Blood cultures x2 negative. Treated with IV vancomycin, ceftriaxone and metronidazole; metronidazole stopped day 7 with no abscess or sinus source. Fever resolved day 4.
- Anticoagulation: heparin infusion from day 1, transitioned to apixaban 5 mg twice daily on day 10. Plan 3 months, then reassess with neurology.
- ICU for 4 days for neurologic checks; headache, chemosis and proptosis improved steadily. At discharge diplopia only at far lateral gaze, acuity improving, papilledema decreasing.
- Hyperglycemia: insulin while inpatient; metformin resumed at discharge.
- PICC placed 4/10.

Discharge medications:
- Vancomycin IV via PICC, dosed by home infusion pharmacy with levels, through 4/27
- Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours via PICC through 4/27
- Apixaban 5 mg twice daily (new)
- Metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, folic acid 1 mg daily, calcium/vitamin D, multivitamin, monthly B12 injections (continue)

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week. Neurology clinic in 8 weeks with repeat MR venogram. Home infusion weekly labs to the hospital ID pharmacist.

Neurology

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
TCM visit, 3 days after discharge. Admitted 3/30-4/13 with bilateral septic cavernous sinus thrombosis after squeezing a pimple on her upper lip. Discharge summary reviewed in full.

Got a ride today. Headache mild, mostly gone. Double vision only looking far to the side, so not driving. Vision 'almost normal'. Eyes much less puffy. Home infusion nurse came yesterday, PICC L arm, no problems. Taking apixaban twice daily, no bleeding. Eating ok. Very tired.

Med rec done: vancomycin and ceftriaxone IV through 4/27, apixaban 5 BID, metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 20, folic acid 1, Ca/D BID, MVI, B12 monthly IM (missed April dose, schedule this week).

Exam: afebrile, HR 80, BP ok. Mild residual lid swelling both sides, no chemosis. EOM full except mild limitation at extreme lateral gaze with diplopia there. Pupils equal and reactive. Facial sensation intact. PICC site clean. Lungs clear, heart RRR. R shin normal.

A/P
1. Cavernous sinus thrombosis, improving. Finish IV antibiotics 4/27. Apixaban for 3 months per neurology. Neurology f/u in June with MRV. No driving until double vision fully gone.
2. Never squeeze facial spots; we talked about it.
3. T2DM: glucose 280 in hospital with infection; BMP today. A1c at next visit.
4. B12 deficiency: nurse visit next week for injection.
5. Cushing syndrome: untreated; I will message endocrinology directly to get her seen.
TCM, high complexity. RTC 2 months, sooner prn.

documents.title: Endocrinology Follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Endocrinology follow-up, seen 05/12/2026.

Ms. Tremblay returns a year after her diagnosis of Cushing syndrome (8 AM cortisol 29 ug/dL, 24-hour urine free cortisol 388 ug/day, L1 compression fracture, low bone density). Interval: B12 deficiency on injections, erysipelas in February, and a hospital stay in March-April for septic cavernous sinus thrombosis, now on apixaban and recovering well.

Exam: central adiposity, faded violaceous striae of the abdomen. Back nontender.

Assessment: Cushing syndrome, source not yet determined. Her recent serious infections make it important to move this forward.

Plan:
1. ACTH level and further testing to localize the source, drawn today; results to follow.
2. Dedicated pituitary MRI to be scheduled once ACTH is back.
3. Continue calcium and vitamin D.
4. Return after testing to discuss treatment.

Endocrinology

reports.text: Contrast-enhanced MR venography of the head. Comparison 03/30/2026. Both cavernous sinuses now enhance normally and symmetrically, without residual filling defect. Superior sagittal, transverse and sigmoid sinuses patent. No new abnormality.

documents.title: Neurology Follow-up
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Neurology clinic, seen 06/08/2026, 10 weeks after admission for bilateral septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.

No headache for over a month. Vision back to her normal; no double vision. No eye swelling. Taking apixaban twice daily without bleeding.

Exam: Acuity 20/20 each eye with glasses. Pupils equal and briskly reactive. Extraocular movements full and painless. No proptosis or chemosis. Fundi: discs flat, no papilledema. Facial sensation normal in all divisions. Rest of neurologic exam normal.

MR venogram 06/01: both cavernous sinuses recanalized.

Assessment: Recovered from septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Plan: Stop apixaban at 3 months, on 06/30/2026. No neurology follow-up needed unless new symptoms.

Neurology

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
F/u, 50F (birthday this month).

Since I saw her in April: IV antibiotics finished 4/27, PICC out. Neurology 6/8: fully recovered, MRV shows both cavernous sinuses open again, stop apixaban today at 3 months. Endocrinology 5/12: ACTH and localization testing drawn, pituitary MRI to follow; she has not heard results yet.

Feels much better. Energy close to normal, tongue fine, no numbness in feet. No headaches, vision normal, back to driving. Bowels: still looser than she'd like, a few a day, but bloating is less since the dilation. Weight steady around 80.
Last apixaban dose this morning.

Meds: metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 20, folic acid 1 mg, Ca/D BID, MVI, B12 1000 mcg IM monthly, apixaban (stopping today). NKDA.

Exam: BP 128/82. Wt 80.6. Eyes: no proptosis, EOM full. Heart RRR, lungs clear. Abd soft, nontender. Skin: R shin normal, no facial lesions. Feet: monofilament and vibration intact, pulses 2+.

A/P
1. Cavernous sinus thrombosis, resolved. Apixaban stopped today per neurology. Off the active list.
2. B12 deficiency anemia: on monthly IM B12; monthly dose given today. She would like to do them at home: RN taught self-injection today, return demonstration good. Rx for vials and syringes sent. CBC, B12, folate today.
3. T2DM: A1c and CMP today. Metformin unchanged.
4. HTN: 128/82, continue lisinopril.
5. Cushing syndrome: endocrinology workup underway. Will watch for their results.
6. Anastomotic stricture: dilated in November, symptoms partly better.
7. HM: just turned 50, Shingrix #1 today, #2 in 2-6 months. Colon screening: resume FIT this fall. Flu/COVID in fall.
RTC 3 months (booked 9/29).
